summary: This primer explains why small and medium-sized enterprises (SMEs) struggle to attract and retain skilled talent and offers strategies to address it. It cites statistics on skills shortages and growth impacts, then covers employer branding, compensation, training, technology, partnerships, remote work, faster hiring, diversity, social media and micro-credentials. Case examples include CoTech Innovations and TechSME.
one_line: A primer on strategies SMEs can use to attract, develop and retain skilled talent despite competition from larger corporations.
key_facts: Approximately 67% of SMEs feel they struggle to find candidates with the appropriate skill sets.
A 2023 survey by the Global SME Forum found that 55% of SMEs saw direct negative impacts on growth due to the talent shortage.
Demand for AI specialists, data analysts and cybersecurity experts has soared with digital transformation.
Josh Harrison, Chief Talent Officer at PeopleStream, said on October 5, 2023 that "Smaller firms frequently lack the brand recognition which can attract applicants, to begin with."
CoTech Innovations, a mid-size tech firm, rebranded in December 2023 and saw a 22% increase in applications from highly qualified candidates the following quarter.
Mary-Anne McCarthy of SME Thrive said "The investment in existing employees typically generates high returns in the form of engagement and retention."
In early 2024, TechSME launched a workforce development program with local universities offering work placements with a pathway to full-time employment.
TechSME CEO Marco Jennings said the program provides a direct talent pipeline and helps shape the curriculum to match industry needs.

Jessica Lin, HR Director at GrowthRapidly SME, said on September 12, 2023 that her firm limited the hiring pipeline to no more than two weeks from initial contact to offer, causing a significant uptick in accepted offers.
Larger corporations often offer better salaries, more comprehensive benefits and career advancement opportunities that SMEs find hard to match.
SMEs can compete with flexible working hours, remote work options and educational allowances.
Offering remote or hybrid positions frees SMEs from geographical constraints and widens the talent pool.
Some SMEs support micro-credential programs so employees can upskill in areas aligned with company needs.
